Road Network Vulnerability with a Case Study: 2024 Noto Earthquake

Student ID: 2554354

1 Introduction

Spatial network data has been introduced to many natural disaster analyses. However, previous research generally focused on the distribution of spatial vulnerabilities against natural disasters and few on the risk generated by spatial features. (Pinto1 et al.2024) Identifying the geographical features that could cause secondary damage is meaningful, for example, a traffic jam potentially hinders aid distribution. This study aims to analyze the vulnerability of a road network and spot the critical nodes for recovery of the road efficiency and capacity when road paths are interrupted due to something such as natural disasters.

This study incorporates a recent disaster that happened on 1st January in Japan, the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake, where the road network was damaged seriously, and the limitation of transportation affected the recovery of the area. (Suppasri et al.2024) Several earthquakes and typhoons hit this region in a few decades, including “the M6.9 Noto-Hanto earthquake that occurred on March 25, 2007” (Nakajima et al.2024). Additionally, the Noto peninsula has a unique geometry, which is elongated in a north-south direction and closure of the root roads can cause hindrance of recovery within the whole peninsula. Identification of critical nodes and edges in this region allows us to have efficient preparedness for mitigating damage and rapid restorations from the damage. Therefore, spatial analysis for vulnerability is required to recover the region after natural disasters.

In addition to the case study, algorithms are introduced into this study to examine whether they can predict road performance correctly. Projections of natural disasters and damages are important in downtown and the disaster-prone areas. Algorithms commonly used for road network analysis and a random method are examined to predict a spatial vulnerability by comparing the case study in the Noto Peninsula.

2.2 Study Area and Dataset

Datasets of the road network were selected including the Noto Peninsula to analyze the road vulnerability. This region was severely affected by the earthquake that occurred on 1st January 2024.

2.2.1 Disaster data (Jan 2024 ~ June 2024)

The daily road status during the recovery phase of the earthquake was provided by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT Japan). The dataset offers restored roads and damaged points from 12th January to 21st March and 25th September. It can be divided into three recovery phases (Early-stage (12th – 18th Jan), Mid-stage (19th Jan – 21st Mar), and Last-stage (25th Sep)) because the change in variable values (nodes and edge numbers, etc.) was observed on only 19th January between 12th January and 21st March.

# create a function to check whether the url is existing 
url_exists <- function(url) {
    status <- tryCatch({          # avoid from stopping the run by errors
        res <- HEAD(url)          # HTTP request (not download)
        res$status_code == 200    # HTTP status code = 200 means success
    }, error = function(e) FALSE) # FALSE will return if an error happens
    return(status)                # return TRUE or FALSE
}

# create consecutive integers 240112 to 240621 representing dates
numbers <- sprintf("%06d", seq(240112, 240621)) 

# get url
valid_urls <- c()
for (num in numbers) {
  url <- paste0("https://www.mlit.go.jp/road/r6noto/", num, "data.zip")
  if (url_exists(url)) {
    valid_urls <- c(valid_urls, url)
  }
}

# download data from the url and unzip files
geojson_data_list <- list()
for (url in valid_urls) {
  # create dates data 
  date_num <- paste0("20", sub(".*\\/([0-9]{6})data.*", "\\1", url))
  date <- as.Date(as.character(date_num), format = "%Y%m%d")
  
  # download file from url
  temp <- tempfile()                             # create a temporary file
  download.file(url, temp, mode = "wb")          # download a url in the temporary file
  unzipped_files <- unzip(temp, list = TRUE)     # unzip a file
  geojson_files <- unzipped_files$Name[grep("\\.geojson$", unzipped_files$Name)] # put only geojson files in `geojson_data_list`
  
  # read the geojson files and add Date column
  geojson_data <- lapply(seq_along(geojson_files), function(i) {
    file <- geojson_files[i]
    # Read files (avoiding error)
    tryCatch({
    data <- st_read(file) %>%
      mutate(Date = date)                        # add Date column
    return(data)          
  }, error = function(e) {
    return(FALSE)         
  })
})
  
  # adjust element names of the list
  list_name <- sub("^json/", "", geojson_files) # remove "json" from the file name
  names(geojson_data) <- list_name              # change the list name of [1] to [5] into json file names
  
  # add one day "geojson_data" to "geojson_data_list"
  if (length(geojson_data) > 0) {
      geojson_data_list[[url]] <- geojson_data
  }
  # delete the temporary file
  unlink(temp)   
}

2.3 Identification of Critical Nodes

Centralities are introduced to identify important nodes in the road network. The degree, betweenness, and closeness centrality of each node are calculated and mapped to compare the three recovery stages and normal times. The nodes with high values of centralities could describe the critical nodes that we should strengthen and restore quickly to deliver relief distribution after disasters.

2.4 Calculation of Network Resilience

To analyze the network vulnerability with interrupted edges, we utilize network resilience that has been introduced to previous studies of transportation network analysis (Taghizadeh et al., 2023; Shen, 2024) Basically, network resilience represents the proportion of recovery at time (t) to total loss at some previous time (td), shown as follows (Henry, 2012); \[ R(t) = \frac{\text{Recovery}(t)}{\text{Loss}(t_d)} \] In this study, the normal times data (OSM road data) is used to compare with recovery because the data of the total loss was not available. Some indices describing network performance are calculated to examine the ratio of recovery to the original ones. To evaluate the resilience of this network, the below indices were introduced by using “igraph” package;

Performance Indices Purpose
Component To identify isolated components
Average Shortest Path Length To measure how efficient it is to move between nodes
Redundancy of Links (Edge Density) To evaluate whether alternative paths are available
Network Efficiency To evaluate the efficiency, like Average Shortest Path Length
Average Centralities (Degree, Betweenness, and Closeness) To examine the features of nodes

The changes in these performance indices over time are compared between three recovery phases and between different calculation methods.

2.5 Algorithm for Resilience Analysis

We also assess network resilience and performance using three node-failure patterns: Random, the breadth-first search (BFS) tree and the depth-first search (DFS) tree, compared to the case study. BFS and DFS are often used in the context of graph traversal. (Jiang, 1990) This study uses these algorithms to predict the closure of road paths, which aims to evaluate whether these algorithms can predict road damage and the status of the road during disasters.

3 Result and Discussion

3.1 Identification of Critical Nodes

3.1.1 Preparing data

To calculate centralities (Degree, Betweenness, Closeness, Eigenvector, and PageRank) at each phase, we prepare the dataset as sf network objects.

3.1.1.1 Recovery Phases

# Network centralities of recovery data
daily_centrality_list <- all_restored_road_sf %>%
  mutate(date = Date) %>%                   # duplicate the date column to leave the date data
  group_by(date) %>%
  group_map(~ {
    network <- as_sfnetwork(.x) %>%
      activate("nodes") %>%
      mutate(degree = degree(.),            # calculate the centrality
             betweenness = betweenness(.),
             closeness = closeness(.),
             eigenvector = eigen_centrality(.)$vector,
             pagerank = page_rank(.)$vector)
    
    st_set_crs(network, 4326) 
    network   # return the network data
  })
names(daily_centrality_list) <- unique(all_restored_road_sf$Date)
head(daily_centrality_list, n = 1)

The graph shows positive correlations between Degree and PageRank, and Betweenness and PageRank. On the other hand, Closeness has negative relationships with other indices and Eigenvector did not show clear correlations with others. Considering the distinction of the Closeness, an increase in connectivity and the number of intermediate points would not imply high efficiency in transportation in this road network. In the following analysis, we focus on the three indices: Degree, Betweenness, and Closeness, due to the clear differences of these features.

3.1.2 Mapping Centralities

3.1.2.1 Preparing the data

# combine the recovery and normal data 
daily_centrality_list$`Normal` = normal_centrality  

# extract only centralites as a tibble object

  lapply(function(x){
    as_tibble(x)
  })

# extract only edge data for mapping
edge_list <- daily_centrality_list %>%            
  lapply(function(x){
    st_as_sf(x, "edges")
  })

# define indices of 4 stages
selected_dates = c("2024-01-12", "2024-01-19", "2024-09-25", "Normal")
stages = c("Early-stage", "Mid-stage", "Last-stage", "Noraml times")
# prepare a ggplot adjustment

  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.direction = "horizontal",
        legend.title = element_blank()) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1, size = 6))

Next, we check Degree centralities to identify the important nodes in terms of connectivity and traffic flows.

In normal times, the yellow plots represent the critical nodes, which are located mostly in the interior. These areas with high value of the Degree can be thought to be important towns where the flow of people and goods is active. In comparison to the normal road status, the nodes around (37.3°N, 136.9°E) in the recovery phases show lower Degree values. It is proposed that the area did not function as usual after the earthquake happened. Furthermore, the degree in the southern part, which is an entrance of the peninsula, decreased dramatically, which can describe the difficulties in the delivery of goods and people for aid. The differences between the Early-stage and Mid-stage cannot be seen in the maps, but nodes around (37.37N, 136.80°E) were repaired considerably at the Last-stage.

3.1.2.3 Betweenness

Following the degree analysis, we measure the betweenness at multiple phases to evaluate the intermediate points in this road network.

# betweenness ----
selected_dates = c("2024-01-12", "2024-01-19", "2024-09-25", "Normal")
b = list()
for(i in 1:4){
  dat = cetrality_tibble_list[selected_dates[i]] %>% bind_rows
  road = edge_list[selected_dates[i]] %>% bind_rows
  
  if(i == 4){
    # separate betweenness into 4 
    breaks <- quantile(dat$betweenness, probs = seq(0, 1, by = 0.25))
    rounded_breaks <- round(breaks, -1) 
    labels <- paste0(head(rounded_breaks, -1), " - ", tail(rounded_breaks, -1))
    dat$betweenness_cat <- cut(dat$betweenness, 
                               breaks = rounded_breaks,
                               labels = labels)
  } else{
    # recovery data have only 0 or 1 betweenness 
    dat$betweenness_cat <- factor(dat$betweenness, level = c(0,1))
  }
  
  
  b[[i]] <- ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = la_cropped, fill = "grey100") +
    geom_sf(data = road, color = "grey", linewidth = 0.3) +   
    geom_sf(data = dat, aes(col = betweenness_cat, size = betweenness_cat)) + 
    ggtitle(paste0(stages[i], " Betweenness")) +
    scale_color_viridis_d(begin  = 0.2, end = 1) +
    scale_size_discrete(range = c(0.5, 2)) +
    option
}
plot_grid(b[[1]], b[[2]], ncol = 2)

plot_grid(b[[3]], b[[4]], ncol = 2)

Normally, there are some nodes with betweenness above 1000 along the multiple roads, which are considered to be prime car roads. On the other hand, many edges during recovery phases show 0 betweenness, and the points with 1 betweenness do not necessarily correspond to the higher betweenness nodes in normal times. It describes that the restored roads might consist of many isolated nodes and there are no alternative roads.

3.1.2.4 Closeness

# closeness ----
selected_dates = c("2024-01-12", "2024-01-19", "2024-09-25", "Normal")
col = viridis(4, option = "D", begin  = 0.1, end = 1) # make a color pallet
c = list()
for(i in 1:4){
  dat = cetrality_tibble_list[selected_dates[i]] %>% bind_rows
  road = edge_list[selected_dates[i]] %>% bind_rows
  
  # split into normal and recovery cases to create color and size scales
  if(i == 4){
    n = 2 # set the legend row number
    # separate closeness into 5 including NA
    breaks <- quantile(dat$closeness[!is.na(dat$closeness)], 
                       probs = seq(0, 1, by = 0.25))
    rounded_breaks <- round(breaks, 3) 
    labels <- paste0(head(rounded_breaks, -1), " - ", tail(rounded_breaks, -1))
    
    dat$closeness_cat <- cut(dat$closeness, 
                             breaks = rounded_breaks, 
                             labels = labels)
    # treat NaN value as isolated nodes
    dat$closeness_cat <- factor(dat$closeness_cat, levels = c(levels(dat$closeness_cat), "no_value"))
    dat$closeness_cat[is.na(dat$closeness_cat)] <- "no_value"
    
    # define the color
    col <- c(viridis(4, option = "D", begin  = 0.1, end = 1), "brown1")
    col_value <- setNames(col, c(levels(dat$closeness_cat)))
    # define the size
    size <- c(0.7, 1, 1.2, 1.5, 0.5)
    size_value <- setNames(size, c(levels(dat$closeness_cat)))
    
  } else{
    n = 1 # set the legend row number

    dat$closeness_round <- round(dat$closeness, 1)
    dat$closeness_round[is.na(dat$closeness_round)] <- NA # conver NaN to NA
    
    dat$closeness_cat <- factor(dat$closeness_round)
    dat$closeness_cat <- factor(dat$closeness_cat, 
                                levels = c(levels(dat$closeness_cat), "no_value"))
    dat$closeness_cat[is.na(dat$closeness_cat)] <- "no_value"
    
    # define the color
    col <- c(viridis(3, option = "D", begin  = 0.1, end = 1), "brown1")
    col_value <- setNames(col, c(levels(dat$closeness_cat)))
    # define the size
    size <-  c(0.4, 0.7, 1, 0.5)
    size_value <- setNames(size, c(levels(dat$closeness_cat)))
  }
  
  c[[i]] <- ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = la_cropped, fill = "grey100") +
    geom_sf(data = road, color = "grey", linewidth = 0.3) +   
    geom_sf(data = dat, aes(col = closeness_cat, size = closeness_cat)) +   
    ggtitle(paste0(stages[i], " Closeness")) +
    scale_color_manual(values = col_value) +  
    scale_size_manual(values = size_value) +
    option +
    guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = n))
}
plot_grid(c[[1]], c[[2]], ncol = 2)

plot_grid(c[[3]], c[[4]], ncol = 2)

In terms of the Closeness centralities, even under usual circumstances, some no_value points can be seen along the north coast and the south area, which means there would be normally isolated nodes and inaccessible nodes from some points. The region inside the peninsula where Betweenness values are lower has a higher Closeness value, which describes that the primary road with long distance stretches inland. During recovery phases, many no_value nodes indicate an increase in isolated points. All values at the three stages are comparatively high (0.3 or more) compared to the normal situation and it can be considered that only short paths existed in this area.

Overall, the result shows many isolated or short paths during recovery phases and implies a great impact of the disaster on the region. High degree points represent some central area and high betweenness describes that the region basically does not have enough alternative roads to access each town. It implies that critical paths with high betweenness require to be strengthened regularly.

3.2 Resilience of Case Study

3.2.1 Preparing the sf object of four phases

Resilience is measured by comparing the changes in some network performance indices over time with those in the original status. Initially, we create the dataset including the road networks at three recovery phases (early, mid, and last stages) and in normal times. At this point, the road type (fclass) and osm_id provided by the osm dataset can be incorporated into the restored road data by identifying the same geometry in the osm road.

# normal times data
normal <- osm_car_roads %>%
  mutate(Stage = "Normal times") %>%     # add Stage column to match to recovery data
  select(osm_id, Stage, fclass, geometry)

# recovery data (only 3 days)
selected_dates <- as.character(selected_dates[-4])
all_restored_road_sf$Date  <- as.character(all_restored_road_sf$Date) # convert Date into character class

selected_recovery <- all_restored_road_sf %>%
  filter(Date %in% selected_dates)  %>%
  mutate(Date = recode(Date,
                      `2024-01-12` = "Early-stage",
                      `2024-01-19` = "Mid-stage",
                      `2024-09-25` = "Last-stage"))  %>%
  dplyr::rename(Stage = Date)

# find the osm_id and fcalss (road type) from normal times data
recovery_fclass <- st_join(selected_recovery, normal[, c("osm_id", "fclass")]) %>%  # join based on geometry
  distinct(Stage, geometry, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%                                   # remove the duplicates rows
  mutate(fclass = ifelse(is.na(fclass), "unclassified", fclass),) %>%               # label unclassified data
  select(osm_id, Stage, fclass, geometry)

# combine the two data
road_sf <- rbind(recovery_fclass, normal)
stages <- c("Early-stage", "Mid-stage", "Last-stage", "Normal times")

# covert osm_id into numeric
road_sf$osm_id <- as.numeric(road_sf$osm_id)

head(road_sf)
## Simple feature collection with 6 features and 3 fields
## Geometry type: LINESTRING
## Dimension:     XY
## Bounding box:  xmin: 136.8686 ymin: 37.14216 xmax: 136.9159 ymax: 37.39444
## Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
##      osm_id       Stage       fclass                       geometry
## 1        NA Early-stage unclassified LINESTRING (136.8707 37.142...
## 2        NA Early-stage unclassified LINESTRING (136.8711 37.143...
## 3 156598584 Early-stage        trunk LINESTRING (136.8703 37.142...
## 4 731921909 Early-stage    secondary LINESTRING (136.8722 37.144...
## 5 127875374 Early-stage        trunk LINESTRING (136.8928 37.388...
## 6 399825820 Early-stage        trunk LINESTRING (136.9046 37.393...
# convert data into LINESTRING for resilience analysis
geom_types <- st_geometry_type(road_sf)
road_lines_sf <- road_sf[geom_types != "POINT", ] # remove point data
road_lines_sf <- st_cast(road_lines_sf, "LINESTRING") # convert into LINESTRING

3.2.2 Calculation of Performance Indices

Each index is calculated in the below code. avg_shortest_path could not be measured using the igraph package because there are many unreachable nodes, and the dodgr package (Padgham, 2019) is introduced to this analysis and calculates the weighted distances.

# define a function for the calculation of performance indices 
performance_calculation <- function(st){
  # filter the road by stages
  sf <- road_lines_sf %>% 
    filter(Stage == st)
  g <- sf %>% 
    as_sfnetwork()
  
  # calculations
  n_nodes = gorder(g) # number of nodes
  n_edges = gsize(g)  # number of edges
  
  ## 1. Components
  components <- components(g)
  n_components <- components$no

  ## 2. Average Shortest Path (Weighted)
  dodgr <- weight_streetnet(sf,                     
                            type_col = "fclass",
                            wt_profile = "motorcar",
                            id_col = "osm_id")
  avg_shortest_path <- mean(dodgr$d_weighted)
  
  ## 3. Edge Density
  edge_density <- edge_density(g)

  ## 4. Network Efficiency
  network_efficiency <- 1 / avg_shortest_path

  ## 5. Average Centralities
  avg_degree <- mean(degree(g))
  avg_betweenness <- mean(betweenness(g))
  avg_closeness <- mean(closeness(g), na.rm = TRUE)

  result <- cbind(st,
                  n_nodes, n_edges, 
                  n_components, 
                  avg_shortest_path , 
                  edge_density, 
                  network_efficiency, 
                  avg_degree, avg_betweenness, avg_closeness)
  
  return(result)
}

performance <- rbind(performance_calculation(stages[1]),
           performance_calculation(stages[2]),
           performance_calculation(stages[3]),
           performance_calculation(stages[4]))

performance <- performance %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate_at(vars(-1), as.numeric)

performance %>% 
  kable(caption = "Performance") %>% 
  column_spec(1:ncol(performance), 
              extra_css = "padding-left: 30px; padding-right: 30px;") %>%
  scroll_box(width = "180%", height = "200px")

This table shows each performance index according to the three recovery phases. Before the analysis of resilience, the basic features in this area are evaluated by comparing performance indices between normal times and recovery phases. The number of edges after the disaster is much fewer than the original one by approximately 1700. It indicated that the earthquake had a great impact on the area and led to a traffic jam and difficulties in aid distribution. Huge gaps can be seen in n_components between recovery and normal times, which means the earthquake interrupted numerous connections and generated isolated edges where the differences between the number of edges and components are only around 20 at three recovery stages. On the other hand, avg_shortest_path and edge_efficiency demonstrate small differences between the 4 stages and the efficiency after the disasters would decline slightly. degree and betweenness centralities in normal times show greater values than recovery phases so the two centralities can be effective indices to evaluate the interruption and recovery from the disasters. Original closeness centrality shows minor value, which describes the poor access between nodes in usual times.

3.2.3 Calculation of Resilience

normal_performance <- unlist(performance[4,-1])
resilience <- sweep(performance[1:3, -1], 2, normal_performance, FUN="/")

resilience_result <- data.frame(Stage = stages[1:3], resilience)

  kable(caption = "Resilience") %>% 
  column_spec(1:ncol(resilience_result),

The resilience was calculated by ratio to the performance in normal times and, in this table, we can examine the change in each index over the restored phase. Basically, an increase in the number of edges results in an increase in efficiency with a shorter minimum path length and connectivity with high centralities and fewer isolated edges. However, in this case, all indices demonstrated contrary patterns to expectations of better road performance. The efficiency of the road (avg_shortest_path, and edge_efficiency) show slight decreases, and increases in n_components and declines in edge_density and centralities describe the setback in the connectivity in this region. It is implied that partial restorations exacerbated the length of respective roads and the importance of the individual nodes.

These maps illustrate the variations in the restored roads. Although the difference between Early-stage and Mid-stage maps cannot be seen clearly, Last-stage demonstrates the repaired area especially around (37.4°N, 136.8°E) and (37.0°N, 136.8°E). In consideration of the decline in connectivity performances, it is suggested that short paths were reconstructed in these regions.

To sum up, it is suggested that the effectivity and the connectivity declined because the increase in short paths and isolated nodes reduced the short average length and component. It was observed that the restoration after disasters was carried out partially in this case. However, we must consider the differences in the resources of restored road data provided by MLIT Japan and the OSM data. The recovery data might not contain all available road paths because they focused on repaired roads, and it is also possible that the OSM data was extracted from four types of roads that ignored some local roads.

3.3 Resilience by Using Algorithms

Following the case study, three methods are incorporated to predict road performance while some edges are disrupted due to certain factors such as disasters.

3.3.1 Preparation of Data

# Convert the road network into an igraph object
road_graph <- osm_car_roads %>%
  as_sfnetwork() %>%
  as.igraph()

# calculation of the number of removed edges in the case study
performance$n_edges <- as.numeric(performance$n_edges)
performance$n_edges[4] - performance$n_edges[1] # [1] 1706
## [1] 1706
performance$n_edges[4] - performance$n_edges[2] # [1] 1701
## [1] 1701
performance$n_edges[4] - performance$n_edges[3] # [1] 1621
## [1] 1621
# define a function for the calculation of performance indices 
al_performance_calculation <- function(g){
  sf = g %>% 
    activate("edges") %>% 
    st_as_sf()
  
  # calculations
  n_nodes = gorder(g) # number of nodes
  n_edges = gsize(g)  # number of edges
  
  ## 1. Components
  components <- components(g)
  n_components <- components$no

  ## 2. Average Shortest Path (Weighted)
  dodgr <- weight_streetnet(sf,                    
                            type_col = "fclass",
                            wt_profile = "motorcar",
                            id_col = "osm_id")
  avg_shortest_path <- mean(dodgr$d_weighted)
  
  ## 3. Edge Density
  edge_density <- edge_density(g)

  ## 4. Network Efficiency 
  network_efficiency <- 1 / avg_shortest_path

  ## 5. Average Centralities
  avg_degree <- mean(degree(g))
  avg_betweenness <- mean(betweenness(g))
  avg_closeness <- mean(closeness(g), na.rm = TRUE)

  result <- cbind(n_nodes, n_edges, 
                  n_components, 
                  avg_shortest_path, 
                  edge_density, 
                  network_efficiency, 
                  avg_degree, avg_betweenness, avg_closeness)
  
  return(result)
}

3.3.1.1 Random

The sample size was set as 5 to examine the accuracy of the prediction, and the number of edges to be eliminated ranged from 1500 to 1700 considering the case study.

set.seed(55)

num_edges_to_remove <- sample(1500:1700, 5)
p_random <- list()
random <- data.frame()

for(i in 1:5){
  # randomly select edges to remove
  random_edges <- sample(E(road_graph), num_edges_to_remove[i])

  # remove the selected edges
  random_removed_graph <- delete_edges(road_graph, random_edges)
  
  # plot the road after the interrupt
  random_removed_graph <- as_sfnetwork(random_removed_graph)
  
  p_random[[i]] <- ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = osm_car_roads, aes(color = "Normal times")) +
    geom_sf(data = st_as_sf(random_removed_graph, "edges"), aes(color = "Restored")) + 
    geom_sf(data = st_as_sf(random_removed_graph, "nodes"), 
            aes(color = "Restored"),
            size = 0.3) +  # plot nodes
    ggtitle(paste0("Random Road Network")) +
    theme_minimal() +
    # theme(legend.position = "none") +
    scale_color_manual(name = "Road", values = c("Normal times" = "brown1", "Restored" = "green3")) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)) + 
    theme(legend.position = "none") 
  
  # calculation of performance 
  dat <- al_performance_calculation(random_removed_graph)
  dat <- dat %>% 
    data.frame() %>% 
    mutate(Algorithm = "Random",
           removed_depth = num_edges_to_remove[i]) %>%
    select(Algorithm, removed_depth, 
           n_nodes, n_edges, 
           n_components, avg_shortest_path, edge_density, network_efficiency,
           avg_degree, avg_betweenness, avg_closeness)
  
  # create a dataframe
  random <- rbind(random, dat)
}

3.3.1.2 BFS

In the BFS method, the depth of searching is set to be from 1500 to 1700 like the Random method, and the starting node is selected from the random 3 points

set.seed(55)

bfs_depth <- sample(1500:1700, 5)
p_bfs <- list()
bfs <- data.frame()

for(i in 1:5){
  # start the BFS from a random node
  start_node <- sample(V(road_graph), 3)
  bfs_result <- bfs(road_graph, root = start_node, order = TRUE)

  # simulate an interrupt by eliminating edges at a random depth level
  edges_to_remove_bfs <- E(road_graph)[.from(bfs_result$order[bfs_result$order <= bfs_depth[i]])]
  bfs_removed_graph <- delete_edges(road_graph, edges_to_remove_bfs)

  # Plot the road after the interrupt
  bfs_removed_graph <- as_sfnetwork(bfs_removed_graph)
  p_bfs[[i]] <- ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = osm_car_roads, aes(color = "Normal times")) +
    geom_sf(data = st_as_sf(bfs_removed_graph, "edges"), aes(color = "Restored")) + 
    geom_sf(data = st_as_sf(bfs_removed_graph, "nodes"), 
            aes(color = "Restored"),
            size = 0.3) +  # plot nodes
    ggtitle(paste0("BFS Road Network")) +
    theme_minimal() +
    # theme(legend.position = "none") +
    scale_color_manual(name = "Road", values = c("Normal times" = "brown1", "Restored" = "green3")) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)) + 
    theme(legend.position = "none")
  
  # calculation of performance
  dat <- al_performance_calculation(bfs_removed_graph)
  dat <- dat %>% 
    data.frame() %>% 
    mutate(Algorithm = "BFS",
           removed_depth = bfs_depth[i]) %>%
    select(Algorithm, removed_depth, 
           n_nodes, n_edges, 
           n_components, avg_shortest_path, edge_density, network_efficiency,
           avg_degree, avg_betweenness, avg_closeness)
  
  # create a dataframe
  bfs <- rbind(bfs, dat)
}

This graph shows each variation in resilience indices calculated by study case, random, BFS, and DFS in response to the proportion of the restored edges to the original ones as the x-axis. BFS and DFS show identical values in all indices when the same nodes are set as the starting points. The reasons could be that the huge depth (1500 to 1700) is set to be about the same as the number of edges in the case study, and there are numerous isolated edges in this original road. Although the orders of the searching nodes were different between BFS and DFS, a large number of removed edges resulted in the same resilience. n_components and edge_density seem to demonstrate a similar trend among the three methods, but this could be because they have a huge deviation from the value in the case study. While Random, BFS, and DFS methods removed only edges, not nodes, the number of nodes in the case study decreased significantly, which could lead to a huge gap between them. Similarly, degree shows the tiny values in all three methods and a large gap from the case study because many nodes after the edge elimination have 0 values. In this graph, as y-values get closer to 1, it means that they approach those in normal times, but avg_shortest_path and network_efficiency describe that the efficiency in the three methods increases along an increase in x-value, though the actual case diminished the road efficiency compared to the original one. This could be because the average of the shortest paths became shorter due to the break of some paths in the three prediction patterns. betweenness and closeness centralities illustrate the close value between the case study and the Random method. BFS and DFS in betweenness show positive correlations with the ratio of repaired edges, but the actual values do not depict a clear relationship with it. The case study in closeness shows almost consistent values, while the closeness of the three methods demonstrates downward trends.

To conclude, compared to other algorithms, the Random method is the best way to predict the vulnerability of the road against disasters. However, there are some trends of Random similar to BFS and DFS and it is difficult to assert that the Random method could adequately predict disrupted roads considering only three samples for the case study as well.

4 Conclusion

This study aimed to identify the critical nodes before and after the disasters in this region and evaluate the methods for the calculation of the vulnerability.

Centralities evaluated the important nodes in this region. The degree could detect the area where there is an active flow of traffic, and the road with the aligned nodes of high betweenness value would describe insufficient alternative paths during disasters. In this case, cities with high traffic flow were observed in northern inland and the essential road ran north-south in the middle of this peninsula. In contrast, the closeness centrality ignored the unreachable nodes, so coastal areas with comparatively short paths showed high closeness values, and the inland road with high betweenness illustrated lower closeness values, which meant the primary road basically was not efficient for accessing another node. Therefore, alternative paths or reinforcement of the main road could be the measures against natural disasters.

The random model predicted the road performance like the case study among all methods, so it could predict the vulnerability in the areas that are subject to natural disasters to a certain degree. The starting point in the BFS and DFS methods did not consider geographical features, and the algorithm focused only on the disruptions not recovery, and they can be potentially improved.

In addition to this, the road data in the original status was used as the total loss in the disasters to calculate the resilience. It is difficult to identify the status immediately after disasters, which could be one of the big issues in network resilience analysis.
